rationale: B wins by a slight margin because it finds the one extra real lane A left on the floor: "Wise says stablecoin rails are cheaper — the open question is who keeps the savings." A's best work is strong, especially "Wise routes cross-border business payments through a regulated stablecoin, skipping correspondent banks," but it mostly stops at the expected payments/trend/regulation trio. B has a small overreach problem, but the public-company pricing-versus-margin angle is grounded enough to matter.
gaps_in_A: A underuses the fact that Wise is "publicly listed and profitable"; it treats that mostly as credibility in "A profitable, public fintech moving £30B a quarter," but misses the sharper investor/pricing question.

The headline "the trend a market's edge case becomes its plumbing" runs ahead of the evidence. A admits the problem with "independent context on other regulated institutions doing the same," which means the headline is doing more work than the facts.

"Wise routes cross-border business payments through a regulated stablecoin, skipping correspondent banks" is a good angle, but "skipping" still needs mechanical proof. A knows this, asking "which leg of the transfer the stablecoin actually replaces," but the headline is a half-step more certain than the update allows.
gaps_in_B: "SWIFT-rail economics" and "which bank fees and float revenue get squeezed" smuggle in bank-economics specifics the update did not supply. That is the one place B starts writing the story before reporting it.
The counterposition angle should demand the same mechanical proof A asks for: which leg of the transfer the stablecoin replaces. B asks for cost and time numbers, but not enough rails mechanics.

"shareholder-versus-mission story" is a strong frame, but it is still an open question, not a demonstrated tension. Without pricing or margin evidence, that line can become a clever second paragraph with no third.
